title: He missed the rest
hookLine: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)
last: ASK — HANDS THE STAGE TO SOMEONE ELSE.

cards: A screenshot arrives with a short note above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you.

It's easy to start drafting the reply right there in your head, point by point, with receipts and a closing line. Section thirty-three of the handbook has a one-line answer for this moment, far older than any screenshot.
It's short, a little ridiculous, and a very good comeback.

teach.b: If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said.

teach.h: HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.
teach.b: Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Why it works: a defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows.

His reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, and nobody else gets hurt by it.
The verb he uses for defend yourself belongs with apologia, a speech of defense, the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial.
Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia.

teach.h: A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.
teach.b: What it isn't: self-hatred, or ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched.
That idea came up a couple of weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face.
It costs nothing, and it ends the conversation better than any receipt.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.

o: a sorry note asking someone to forgive a mistake
a speech of defense, answering charges point by point
a joke you make at your own expense to calm things

games.q: he missed the rest — tap the pairs.
p: he didn't know my other faults

s: Epictetus advises a careful point-by-point defense
he says don't defend yourself at all, and answer with a joke on yourself.
Epictetus' answer says the critic missed some of your faults
he didn't know my other faults, or he'd have mentioned more than these.

games.q: a friend tells you someone has been criticizing you. what does Epictetus suggest you say?
o: send a full rebuttal, with screenshots.
he didn't know my other faults, or he'd have mentioned them too.
games.why: the reply steps out of the contest. it agrees you have faults, more than the critic knows, so there's nothing left to fight.

practice: Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, and notice where it lands in your body, and the urge to argue with it. Then try Epictetus' answer inside, he missed the rest, and see if the sting changes; you might even smile.
If part of it was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go.

wordCard.voice: Apologia. The Greek word for a speech of defense, which Epictetus says to skip: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a speech of defense. Epictetus uses the related verb: don't defend yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: better than any receipt. A fair point teaches; a wrong one can't touch what's yours. Day three hundred sixty-eight, done.
